title: Radiation shelter for a solar particle event
steps: Stop your current task and secure loose items.
Move to the designated shelter area in the centre of the cabin.
Empty the nearby stowage bays and pack the bags, food and water along the least shielded wall, to put more mass between you and the particles.
Aim to have the shelter built within 1 hour of the alert.
Stay inside until the radiation alert clears. This can take up to 24 hours.
Keep wearing your personal dosimeter and check its readings.
escalate_if: The dose rate keeps rising after the shelter is built.
A crew member feels unwell while sheltering: alert the crew medical officer.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA, Scientists and Engineers Evaluate Orion Radiation Protection Plan, https://www.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/orion/scientists-and-engineers-evaluate-orion-radiation-protection-plan/ ; NASA Science, To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun, https://science.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-2/to-protect-artemis-ii-astronauts-nasa-experts-keep-eyes-on-sun/

title: Fatigue recovery
steps: Protect your next scheduled sleep period, and keep to a regular sleep and wake time.
Before sleep, switch to the dim, warm pre-sleep lighting and avoid bright screens.
After waking, use bright light to help you become alert.
Do critical tasks more slowly, follow the checklist step by step, and ask a crewmate to cross-check your work.
Tell the crew medical officer if the fatigue does not improve.
escalate_if: Fatigue continues after protected sleep.
You make a fatigue-related mistake on a critical task.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA NTRS, Scheuring, Moomaw and Johnston, Fatigue in U.S. Astronauts Onboard the ISS, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150009487/downloads/20150009487.pdf ; NASA NTRS, Subjective Sleep Experience During Shuttle Missions, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20120007773/downloads/20120007773.pdf ; NASA Ames Fatigue Countermeasures Laboratory, https://humansystems.arc.nasa.gov/groups/fatigue/

title: High cabin CO2
steps: Check that the cabin air fans are running, and move to a module with better air flow.
Check the CO2 scrubber and report the fault to the ground team.
NASA limits cabin CO2 to a one-hour average of no more than 3 mmHg.
On the ISS, each 1 mmHg rise in CO2 doubled the odds of a crew member reporting a headache.
Report headaches, tiredness or trouble concentrating to the crew medical officer.
Slow down on critical tasks and cross-check each other's work until CO2 is back under the limit.
escalate_if: CO2 keeps rising, or reaches 5.3 mmHg.
Anyone has trouble breathing: use the breathing difficulty card.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA OCHMO Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-004-carbon-dioxide.pdf ; NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 [V2 6004] (one-hour average no more than 3 mmHg), https://www.nasa.gov/reference/6-0-natural-and-induced-environments-vol-2 ; NASA NTRS, The Relationship Between CO2 Levels and CO2 Related Symptoms Reported on the ISS (Foy, Law et al. 2014: odds of headache double per 1 mmHg), http://hdl.handle.net/2060/20140003857 ; NASA NTRS, CO2 on the International Space Station: An Operations Update (missed steps and headaches with rising CO2), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20150019624.pdf ; NASA NTRS 20100036637 (180-day SMAC 0.7% = 5.3 mmHg), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20100036637

title: Chest pain
steps: Stop all activity and stay still. Anchor yourself, or have a crewmate hold you in place.
Alert the crew medical officer now.
Loosen anything tight around the neck and waist.
The crew medical officer opens the onboard medical checklist and decides on any medication.
Bring the defibrillator, and be ready to start chest compressions if the person stops responding.
Send a report to the flight surgeon. Replies from Earth take minutes, so do not wait before acting.
Treat chest pain that does not go away as an emergency.
escalate_if: The person stops responding or stops breathing normally: use the unresponsive card.
The pain spreads to the arms, neck, jaw or back, or comes with breathlessness or sweating.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NHS, Chest pain, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/chest-pain/ ; British Red Cross, Heart attack first aid, https://www.redcross.org.uk/first-aid/learn-first-aid/heart-attack ; NASA NTRS, ISS medical kit and crew medical officer role, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110010924/downloads/20110010924.pdf

title: Breathing difficulty
steps: If more than one person is affected, or you smell smoke or chemicals, treat it as a cabin atmosphere emergency: put on a breathing mask now and sound the alarm.
Alert the crew medical officer.
Keep the person still and calm.
The crew medical officer follows the onboard medical checklist and can give oxygen from the medical kit.
Send a report to the flight surgeon.
escalate_if: The person stops breathing normally or stops responding: use the unresponsive card.
Other crew start to feel unwell: treat it as a cabin atmosphere emergency.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA NTRS, Emergency Operations History, ISS (rapid depressurization, fire, toxic atmosphere, medical), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20220019247/downloads/Emergency%20Ops%20History%20for%20SpaceOps%20Conference%202023.pdf ; NASA NTRS, ISS Fire Detection and Suppression incl. Portable Breathing Apparatus, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20030053429/downloads/20030053429.pdf ; NASA NTRS, ISS medical kit (oxygen supplementation), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110010924/downloads/20110010924.pdf

title: FAST check: face, arms, speech
steps: Face: has one side of the face fallen? Can they smile?
Arms: can they raise both arms and keep them there?
Speech: is their speech slurred or confused?
If you see any one of these signs, alert the crew medical officer now.
Note the time the signs started.
Report the signs even if they go away.
Send the FAST findings to the flight surgeon.
escalate_if: The person stops responding: use the unresponsive card.
A sudden, severe headache.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NHS, Act FAST, https://www.nhs.uk/actFAST ; British Heart Foundation, Stroke, https://www.bhf.org.uk/informationsupport/conditions/stroke ; adapted for spaceflight: the crew medical officer replaces calling 999

title: Unresponsive crew member
steps: Check for a response and for normal breathing.
Sound the alarm and alert the crew medical officer.
If they are not breathing normally, start chest compressions now using the Evetts-Russomano method, bracing yourself against their body.
Bring the defibrillator and use it as soon as it is ready.
When help arrives, strap the person to the crew medical restraint system and continue compressions using the handstand method.
Swap rescuers often. Compressions in weightlessness are tiring.
Send a report to the flight surgeon.
escalate_if: Normal breathing does not return: keep going until the crew medical officer says to stop.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. Hinkelbein et al. 2020, Cardiopulmonary resuscitation during spaceflight: a guideline for CPR in microgravity (DGLRM and ESAM-SMG), https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-020-00793-y ; NASA NTRS, CPR in microgravity and the Crew Medical Restraint System, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150020975/downloads/20150020975.pdf

title: Severe bleeding
steps: Put on gloves and press firmly and directly on the wound with a dressing.
Keep the pressure on.
Alert the crew medical officer.
Restrain the injured person so you can keep steady pressure.
In weightlessness, blood forms droplets that drift. Keep them away from the eyes, nose and mouth, and catch them with absorbent material.
Send a report to the flight surgeon.
escalate_if: The bleeding does not slow with firm pressure.
The person stops responding: use the unresponsive card.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA NTRS, Extraterrestrial Hemorrhage Control (direct pressure on all compressible bleeding), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20110011168.pdf ; Scientific American, fluid-filled domes for bleeding in deep-space flight (blood droplets in microgravity), https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/during-medical-emergencies-on-deep-space-flights-fluid-filled-domes-could-stanch-bleeding/

title: Suspected broken bone
steps: Stop the activity and keep the injured part still.
Restrain the injured person so they do not drift.
Alert the crew medical officer.
The crew medical officer immobilises the injury using the onboard medical kit and checklist.
If there is bleeding, also use the severe bleeding card.
Send a report to the flight surgeon, with photos or ultrasound images if possible.
escalate_if: Bleeding that does not stop: use the severe bleeding card.
The person stops responding: use the unresponsive card.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA NTRS, ISS medical kit and crew medical officer role, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110010924/downloads/20110010924.pdf ; Healthcare IT News, how ISS telemedicine sends images and ultrasound to flight surgeons, https://www.healthcareitnews.com/news/international-space-station-teaches-healthcare-about-telemedicine

title: Medical emergency
steps: Sound the alarm and alert the crew medical officer.
Make the area safe: secure loose equipment and restrain the person so they do not drift.
Stay with them and keep them calm.
The crew medical officer opens the onboard medical checklist.
Send a report to the flight surgeon. On a Mars mission replies take minutes, so act on the checklist without waiting.
escalate_if: Not breathing normally: use the unresponsive card.
Heavy bleeding: use the severe bleeding card.
Chest pain: use the chest pain card.
source: Demonstration content, not medical advice. NASA NTRS, ISS emergency response training (crews must act without mission control), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20120002562/downloads/20120002562.pdf ; NASA NTRS, ISS medical kit and crew medical officer role, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110010924/downloads/20110010924.pdf
